errorMonitoring.title: Error monitoring
errorMonitoring.intro: We use the error monitoring service Sentry so that we can diagnose crashes and unexpected errors, on both the website and the API. When an error occurs, the following goes to Sentry:
errorMonitoring.item1: The error itself: its message and the technical stack trace.
errorMonitoring.item2: The address of the page the error happened on, plus browser and operating system details.
errorMonitoring.item3: The IP address of your connection.
errorMonitoring.recipient: Recipient: Sentry (Functional Software, Inc.). The records are processed on Sentry's European Union (Germany) infrastructure.
errorMonitoring.legalBasis: Legal basis: legitimate interest — keeping the service secure and available, and finding and fixing faults.
errorMonitoring.limits: We deliberately keep session replay and performance tracing switched off: your screen is not recorded, your browsing behaviour is not tracked, and your form contents are not sent. Your application data, your CV and email contents are never included in an error record.
errorMonitoring.retention: Error records are deleted when Sentry's retention period expires; the error records themselves are never written to the product's own database. (The one place the product's database does keep your IP address is the "Request log" item above.)

visitCounter.title: Visit counter
visitCounter.intro: We count how often public pages are opened, on our own server. A visit records only:
visitCounter.item1: The address of the public page opened (everything after the question mark excluded) and the page's language.
visitCounter.item2: Which site you found us from — the domain only.
visitCounter.item3: A daily counter — how many times that combination was seen that day.
visitCounter.recipient: Recipient: none. The data stays on our own server; it is sent to no analytics service and to no other third party.
visitCounter.legalBasis: No stored row can be linked to a person — no visitor id, no session id, no IP address, no browser details — so there is no personal data here. Should it be assessed otherwise, the basis is legitimate interest (KVKK art. 5/2-f, GDPR art. 6/1-f): measuring whether the service is used at all.
visitCounter.limits: No cookie is used, nothing is written to your browser, and there is no profiling or ad targeting. If your browser has “Do Not Track” switched on, nothing is counted. See “Visit counter” in the Cookie Policy for the details.
visitCounter.retention: Retention: the rows are aggregate counts holding no personal data, so they are kept indefinitely.

dataCollection.title: What data we collect and why
dataCollection.intro: e-kariyerim is a personal tool that helps you track your job applications. To provide the service, we process the following data:
dataCollection.item1: Account details: email address and password (stored hashed); first and last name are optional — the sign-up form does not ask for them, you can add them under Settings. If you sign in with Google, LinkedIn or GitHub, that account's identifier is stored instead of a password (see below).
dataCollection.item2: Application data you enter or import: company, job listing, application status, dates, and notes.
dataCollection.item3: Reminders derived from this data (follow-up suggestions, no-response alerts).
dataCollection.item4: If you turn on Gmail Scanning (an opt-in browser-extension feature), the subject line and a short snippet of a detected status-update email — used to detect a status change and, for a job not yet tracked, to read off the company/role — are stored on your account and, for that detection, sent to OpenAI. This content is first evaluated locally in your browser; only a message that looks job-application-related ever reaches us. See "Cross-border data transfer" below.
dataCollection.outro: Apart from the request log, this data is used solely to provide you with application tracking and personal analytics features; the request log serves only the security and legal purposes listed above.
dataCollection.item5: An HR contact you keep for an application or a job you track: name, email address and LinkedIn profile URL. You can enter these yourself; in addition, when you match a status-update email to an application and confirm it, that email's sender address may be filled in as the HR email — automated mailboxes (no-reply and the like) and job-platform addresses are never stored for this, and an address filled this way is labelled "from an incoming email" in the interface. Only you can see it; it is never shown to other users, never included in any analytics, never sent anywhere, and it is deleted along with the application or your account. We never email that address on our own — in the interface it is only a link.
dataCollection.item6: Request log: for every request in which you send something to the site — sign-up, sign-in, adding or editing an application, importing, uploading a CV, a company review, a salary entry, a candidate experience, a blog comment, feedback and the like — the IP address of your connection, the request path, its outcome and the time. This log is kept solely for the security of your account, for fighting abuse and for our legal obligations (such as a properly made request from a competent authority); it is never shown on any screen, report or data export, and it is deleted together with your account. The same log is kept on the surfaces that need no sign-in (CV scan, benchmark) and for failed sign-in attempts; as those belong to no account, they are deleted after 12 months. What is not logged: page views (see "Visit counter").
dataCollection.item7: If you use the weekly job matching (a paid feature): the job titles (up to three) and the location you save as your search criteria. They are stored on your account and, once a week, used as a search on LinkedIn and kariyer.net — see "Cross-border data transfer" below. The postings found are kept for you for a limited time; which ones you already applied to is worked out from your own applications and never stored as a separate record. If you also give consent, the fit score computed for each posting, its short reasoning and the matched/missing criteria are kept on your account too — see "Weekly job matching".

googleSignIn.title: Sign in with Google
googleSignIn.intro: Sign in with Google is an optional login method, an alternative to registering with email and password. When you use it, we receive only the following from Google:
googleSignIn.item1: Your Google account's permanent identifier (so we can recognise your account even if your email address changes).
googleSignIn.item2: Your email address, as verified by Google.
googleSignIn.item3: The first and last name on your Google profile (pre-filled in the sign-up form; you can change them before saving).
googleSignIn.noAccess: We do not access, and never request permission for, your Gmail, contacts, Drive or any other data in your Google account. We do not store the access tokens Google issues us; they are discarded as soon as sign-in completes.
googleSignIn.linking: If the verified email address of your Google account already belongs to an e-kariyerim account created with a password, the Google sign-in is linked to that account and signs you into it; your password keeps working.
googleSignIn.revoke: You can remove the permission on Google's side at any time under Google Account → Security → Third-party apps. Deleting your e-kariyerim account also removes the link to Google.

linkedInSignIn.title: Sign in with LinkedIn
linkedInSignIn.intro: Sign in with LinkedIn is an optional login method, an alternative to registering with email and password. When you use it, we receive only the following from LinkedIn:
linkedInSignIn.item1: Your LinkedIn account's permanent identifier (so we can recognise your account even if your email address changes).
linkedInSignIn.item2: Your email address, as verified by LinkedIn — if LinkedIn shares it. LinkedIn does not always do so; in that case we ask you to enter an email address yourself when you complete your sign-up, and that address is not verified by us.
linkedInSignIn.item3: The first and last name on your LinkedIn profile (pre-filled in the sign-up form; you can change them before saving).
linkedInSignIn.noAccess: We do not access, and never request permission for, your connections, messages, posts or any other data in your LinkedIn account. We do not store the access tokens LinkedIn issues us; they are discarded as soon as sign-in completes.
linkedInSignIn.linking: If the email address verified by LinkedIn already belongs to an e-kariyerim account created with a password, the LinkedIn sign-in is linked to that account and signs you into it; your password keeps working. An email address you typed in yourself is never used to link to an existing account.
linkedInSignIn.revoke: You can remove the permission on LinkedIn's side at any time under Settings & Privacy → Data privacy → Other applications → Permitted services. Deleting your e-kariyerim account also removes the link to LinkedIn.

gitHubSignIn.title: Sign in with GitHub
gitHubSignIn.intro: Sign in with GitHub is an optional login method, an alternative to registering with email and password. When you use it, we receive only the following from GitHub:
gitHubSignIn.item1: Your GitHub account's numeric identifier (so we can recognise your account even if you change your username or email address).
gitHubSignIn.item2: Your email address, as verified by GitHub — if GitHub shares one. An account that keeps its address private shares none; in that case we ask you to enter an email address yourself when you complete your sign-up, and that address is not verified by us.
gitHubSignIn.item3: The display name on your GitHub profile, split into a first and last name (pre-filled in the sign-up form; you can change them before saving).
gitHubSignIn.noAccess: We ask GitHub for two permissions only — read your profile and read your email addresses. We do not access, and never request permission for, your repositories (public or private), your code, your issues or anything else in your GitHub account. We do not store the access tokens GitHub issues us; they are discarded as soon as sign-in completes.
gitHubSignIn.linking: If the email address verified by GitHub already belongs to an e-kariyerim account created with a password, the GitHub sign-in is linked to that account and signs you into it; your password keeps working. An email address you typed in yourself is never used to link to an existing account.
gitHubSignIn.revoke: You can remove the permission on GitHub's side at any time under Settings → Applications → Authorized OAuth Apps. Deleting your e-kariyerim account also removes the link to GitHub.

crossBorderTransfer.title: Cross-border data transfer
crossBorderTransfer.intro: Your data goes abroad in three cases. The first is Gmail Scanning: if you turn it on, the subject line and a short summary of each detected status-update email are sent abroad to work out what it means for your application.
crossBorderTransfer.recipient: Recipient: OpenAI, L.L.C. (United States) — our API provider.
crossBorderTransfer.purpose: Purpose: to classify the email's application-status signal, and — for a job not yet tracked — to read off a company name and job title; this only runs when a simpler, local rule-based check doesn't already recognize the email.
crossBorderTransfer.legalBasis: Legal basis: this only happens for Gmail Scanning you turn on yourself in the browser extension; nothing is sent unless you use this feature.
crossBorderTransfer.withdraw: Withdrawal: turn off Gmail Scanning in the browser extension's Settings page. Or delete your account, to stop this entirely.
crossBorderTransfer.sensitiveDataNote: The subject and snippet are also stored on your account (visible to you when reviewing a suggestion) — never the full email body.
crossBorderTransfer.feedbackTransfer: The second is feedback: when you send feedback from inside the app, your message and its technical context are copied to a private repository on GitHub so it can be tracked. Recipient: GitHub, Inc. (Microsoft, United States). Your name, your account email address and your reply address are not sent. Lawful basis: legitimate interest — tracking and fixing what users report. See the "Feedback you send" section above for the detail.
crossBorderTransfer.jobSourceTransfer: The third is the weekly job matching (a paid feature): once a week, the job titles and the location you saved as criteria are sent as a search query to LinkedIn, and the public job postings it lists are fetched. Recipient: LinkedIn Ireland Unlimited Company (Ireland; LinkedIn Corporation, United States). The same search also goes to kariyer.net in Türkiye (Kariyer.net Elektronik Yayıncılık ve İletişim Hizmetleri A.Ş., Istanbul); that is not a cross-border transfer and is mentioned here for completeness. What is sent is the search itself — a job title and a place — and nothing else: not your name, not your account, not your CV. Lawful basis: this only happens for criteria you saved yourself, while your paid plan is active; delete the criteria or let the plan lapse and it stops. Withdrawal: remove your criteria from the job matching settings, or delete your account.

browserExtension.title: Browser extension
browserExtension.before: What the browser extension reads on your own device, what it stores, and what it sends is described in a separate document:
browserExtension.after: If you haven't installed the extension, that document doesn't apply to you.

retention.title: Retention period
retention.body: Data tied to your account is kept until you delete your account; no automatic time-based deletion is applied to it. The one exception is request-log entries that belong to no account (an anonymous CV scan, a benchmark answer, a failed sign-in attempt): those are deleted automatically after 12 months.

rights.title: Your rights
rights.before: You can export a copy of your data or permanently delete your account at any time. You can do this from the
rights.after: page. Deleting your account permanently removes every piece of data belonging to it — your applications, your tracked jobs, your CVs, your imports, your reminders, your email suggestions and notifications, your company reviews, the salary entries you shared, your candidate experiences, your blog comments, the feedback you sent and your request log. The request log is not part of the export file; to access your own entries, write to privacy@ekariyerim.com.

cvStorage.title: CVs you upload
cvStorage.intro: Uploading a CV is entirely optional; the rest of the service works without one. When you do upload a CV:
cvStorage.where: The file is stored in a bucket closed to the public on Google Cloud in the European Union region (europe-west1) — the same region as your account and application data. Even a guessed address cannot reach it; the bucket is not exposed to the internet at all.
cvStorage.access: Only you, while signed in, can reach the file. Every download is checked against your own account and streamed through the e-kariyerim server; no shareable or time-limited link is ever produced. It is never shown to other users, to employers or to job boards.
cvStorage.noTransfer: The contents of your CV are never sent to any third party, AI services included. The one exception is the paid feature described under "Weekly job matching" below, which you turn on yourself and consent to separately; then only the text of your default CV is sent, and only for scoring. The file is not read, converted to text or analysed; it is only stored and handed back to you. The first-page preview you see on the My CVs page is rendered in your own browser, not on the server.
cvStorage.deletion: A CV you delete is deleted permanently — the storage-side recovery window is deliberately turned off. Deleting your account deletes all of your CVs with it.
cvStorage.readability: If you choose to, you can measure an uploaded CV's ATS readability (the button on the My CVs page). These are the same checks as the sign-in-free CV scan and they run on our server; nothing is sent to an AI model. The report (score, findings, the lines they point at and the text extracted from the file) is produced only when you ask, kept next to that CV, visible only to you, and deleted together with the CV. The data export carries the score and the date it was measured.
cvStorage.sensitiveDataNote: A CV can carry more than your work history — a photo, a date of birth, or health or military-service information — which is why we ask for your explicit consent before each upload. What goes into it is your decision: none of those fields are needed for the service to work, and you can delete the file at any time.
cvStorage.consent: The lawful basis is your explicit consent, and it is taken separately for every upload: you tick the consent box before choosing a file, the box is never pre-ticked, and it clears again after each upload. You can withdraw consent at any time by deleting the file, and deleting your account deletes all of your CVs with it.

cvScan.title: CV scan (without signing in)
cvScan.intro: On the public CV scan page you can upload a PDF or Word file and see what an applicant tracking system reads from it. This is separate from, and different to, "CVs you upload" above:
cvScan.noStorage: The file is not stored anywhere. It is never written to disk on the server and never placed in storage; it exists in memory for the length of the request and is gone once the response is sent. The text of your CV is not kept either.
cvScan.retained: Three things survive a scan: your IP address (in memory for 2 hours to enforce the scan limit; and, as the security record described under "Request log" above, for 12 months — never linked to the score), an anonymous score (a number from 0 to 100, with no record of which file it came from or whose it was), and a scan counter.
cvScan.noTransfer: All seven checks behind the score run on our own server: the score is never asked of an AI model, so it cannot be inflated by an instruction written inside the CV. Unless you tick the optional box, the contents of your CV are not sent to any third party.
cvScan.contentNotes: If you ask for notes on the writing (the second, optional box): the text of your CV is sent to Google Cloud Vertex AI — in the EU region our infrastructure already runs in, with the same processor; no new country is involved. It goes through paid Vertex, which does not train on the content. The notes do not affect the score, the text is still stored nowhere, and with the box unticked no model is involved at all.
cvScan.output: The excerpts and the raw text you see on the result screen exist only inside the response to your own request; they are not recorded and never written to logs.
cvScan.consent: The legal basis is your explicit consent, taken separately for every scan: the box is never pre-ticked and is cleared again after each scan. The second box, for the content notes, is separate and genuinely optional — the scan works fully without it and your score is identical. Since nothing is stored, there is no retention to withdraw; not running the scan is enough.

jobMatching.title: Weekly job matching (a paid feature)
jobMatching.intro: With the Pro plan and the search criteria you saved, new LinkedIn and kariyer.net postings are searched every Monday (for the criteria going to the two sites see "Cross-border data transfer"). Each posting found is compared with your default CV and scored — only if you separately consent:
jobMatching.what: What is sent: the text of your default CV (not the file; the first 15,000 characters) together with the text of one posting. Recipient: Google Cloud Vertex AI, in the EU region our infrastructure already runs in (europe-west1) and with the same processor — no new country and no new processor is involved. It goes through paid Vertex, which does not train on the content and does not keep it.
jobMatching.kept: What we keep: for each posting a 0–100 fit score, a sentence or two of reasoning, the lists of matched and missing criteria and the skills the posting asks for — on your account, next to the posting. The CV text itself is written nowhere: it is read again from your stored file every week and lives in memory for the length of the request. To track the cost of the calls, how many tokens were spent for which feature is also recorded against your account; that record holds no text and survives account deletion (detached from your identity).
jobMatching.consent: The lawful basis is your explicit consent, given when you first save your criteria through a box that is never pre-ticked; the moment it was given is recorded and shown on the criteria page. Criteria cannot be saved without it, because there is no version of the feature without scoring.
jobMatching.withdraw: Withdrawal: delete your criteria — the search and the scoring stop at once, that week's list and scores are deleted, and your CV is never sent again. Deleting your account has the same effect.

feedback.title: Feedback you send
feedback.intro: The feedback button in the bottom-right corner of every page is entirely optional. When you send a message:
feedback.what: Your message, the topic you picked (bug/idea/question) and, if you chose one, how you said it was going are stored against your account.
feedback.context: Technical context is stored with it: the path of the page you opened the panel from (for example /en/applications), your language and theme, and your browser details. Only the path of the address is taken — query parameters (an application id, say) are dropped both in your browser and on the server.
feedback.notCollected: The contents of your applications, CVs and emails are not sent with feedback, and no screenshot is taken.
feedback.replyEmail: The reply address is optional and can be left blank; it is used only to get back to you, never for marketing.
feedback.deletion: Deleting your account deletes your feedback from our database. The tracking record on GitHub never carried your identity, so after that deletion it can no longer be traced back to you; if you would like that record removed as well, just write to us.
feedback.legalBasis: Lawful basis: legitimate interest — fixing and improving the product against what users report.
feedback.mirror: Your message and the technical context above are also opened as a tracking record in a private repository on GitHub, so we can follow it through. Your name, your account email address and your reply address are not sent there — only the record's id goes, so seeing who wrote it means looking it up in our own database.
feedback.mirrorRecipient: Recipient: GitHub, Inc. (Microsoft, United States). This is a transfer abroad; see the "Transfers abroad" section below.
feedback.storage: Feedback is stored in our own database; the canonical record is ours.

companyReviews.title: Company reviews you write
companyReviews.intro: Writing a review of a company is optional and needs an account. When you do:
companyReviews.what: Your review — your overall rating, the optional area ratings, the ready-made statements you picked and your relationship to the company (current employee, former employee, intern) — is stored against your account, together with its moderation status and any note a moderator wrote. There is no free text in a review since 16 September 2026; if you wrote one before then, its title, pros and cons stay stored for you and are no longer shown to anyone else.
companyReviews.anonymous: Published reviews never show your name, email or account; readers see the ratings, the statements, your relationship to the company and the month it was written. The month rather than the day, on purpose: a date is one more clue to who wrote it.
companyReviews.admin: A moderator who looks at your review — after a report, or for a review from before the switch — can see the account behind it. That is what makes moderation possible, and it is the only place your identity meets your review.
companyReviews.reports: If you report someone else's review, the report (reason, your note, the time) is stored against your account and shown to the moderator. The review's author never sees who reported it.
companyReviews.helpful: Marking a review helpful is stored as one row per review per account, so it can be undone and cannot be counted twice. Nobody sees who marked what.
companyReviews.storage: Reviews, reports and helpful marks are stored in our own database and are not sent to any third party.
companyReviews.deletion: Deleting your account deletes your reviews, your reports and your helpful marks. Reviews you wrote disappear from the company pages and from the company's score; this is also what your data export contains.
companyReviews.legalBasis: Lawful basis: your explicit action — you choose to write, report or mark — and, for moderation, legitimate interest: keeping what is published about a named company fair and lawful.

payments.title: Payments (Pro plan)
payments.intro: When you buy the Pro plan, the payment is taken on the secure payment page of PayTR Ödeme ve Elektronik Para Kuruluşu A.Ş.
payments.card: Your card number, expiry date and security code never reach e-kariyerim; they are entered on PayTR's page and processed there.
payments.sent: What we send PayTR: your e-mail address, the name, address and phone number you enter at checkout, the IP address of the connection you start the payment from, the chosen plan and the amount.
payments.kept: What we keep: the order record (plan, amount, date, outcome), the name, address and phone number you entered for the invoice, the result PayTR reported and, if any, the failure reason. The IP address of PayTR's server call that reports the result is recorded too and never shown anywhere.
payments.retention: Payment and invoicing records are kept for the retention period the tax legislation requires. If you delete your account, these records are detached from it (the link to your identity is removed) but not deleted until that period ends.
payments.refunds: Refunds are made only through our own system, via PayTR's refund service, to the card you paid with; your request and its outcome are kept on the order record.
payments.provider: PayTR is the data controller for the data it processes itself; its privacy notice is published at paytr.com.
payments.legalBasis: Legal basis: performance of the contract (KVKK art. 5/2-c) and compliance with a legal obligation (art. 5/2-ç).

companySalaries.title: Salary information you share
companySalaries.intro: Sharing your salary at a company is optional and requires an account. When you do:
companySalaries.what: Your entry — the occupation you picked from the list, total years of experience, employment type, whether you are a current or former employee, the years of the period you drew the salary in, monthly net salary with its currency, and the annual bonus if any — is stored linked to your account. There is no free text: the occupation comes from a catalogue based on ISCO-08.
companySalaries.whoSees: Entries are shown only to signed-in users; the public company page says only how many entries there are.
companySalaries.band: Readers see an experience band (0–1, 2–4, 5–9, 10+) rather than your exact years, and the period of the salary in years rather than a date or a month. Deliberately: together with an occupation, the exact years and date would give away who wrote it at a small company.
companySalaries.noAuthor: A published entry never shows your name, e-mail or account, and contains nothing you typed. Only we can see the account behind an entry.
companySalaries.storage: Entries are stored in our own database and are not sent to any third party.
companySalaries.deletion: You can delete an entry from My contributions at any time. Deleting your account deletes all of them; your data export includes them with the exact years.
companySalaries.legalBasis: Legal basis: your explicit action — you choose to share.

candidateExperiences.title: The candidate experiences you share
candidateExperiences.intro: Rating a company's hiring process is optional and needs an account. When you do:
candidateExperiences.what: Your entry — your overall rating, the areas you rated, the statements you picked from the ready-made list and, if you answered them, the outcome, length, number of stages and interview types — is stored against your account. There is no free text: every published sentence is one of our own fixed statements.
candidateExperiences.whoSees: Entries are shown on the public company page: the ratings, the statements and the process tags. The score, the area averages and the process statistics appear once a company has at least three entries.
candidateExperiences.quarter: Readers see the quarter only (2026 Q3), never the day or the month; a job title, an interviewer or a team name is never asked. Deliberately: a company knows whom it interviewed, and a month with a title would give away who wrote it at a small company.
candidateExperiences.noAuthor: A published entry never shows your name, e-mail or account. Only we can see the account behind it.
candidateExperiences.storage: Entries are kept in our own database; nothing is sent to any third party.
candidateExperiences.deletion: You can delete an entry at any time from My contributions. Deleting your account deletes all of them; your data export includes them with their exact dates.
candidateExperiences.legalBasis: Legal basis: your explicit action — you choose to share.

blogComments.title: The comments you write on blog posts
blogComments.intro: Commenting on a blog post is optional and needs an account. When you do:
blogComments.what: Your comment is kept as plain text, tied to your account, with when it was written and edited and its moderation status. Every comment is visible only to you until an admin approves it; a comment that is not approved is never published.
blogComments.name: A published comment shows your first name and the initial of your last name (for example "Selin Y."); an account with no name shows "A reader". Your e-mail address, your account and anything else about you are never shown. Everyone who reads the post sees that name — know this before you write.
blogComments.noEdit: An approved comment can be neither changed nor deleted: others have replied to it. While it waits for approval you can edit it from My contributions or under the post.
blogComments.moderation: The admin who reviews your comment sees the account behind it; that is what makes moderation possible, and it is the only place your identity meets your comment. If you report a comment, the report (reason, your note, time) is kept against your account and shown only to admins; the comment's author never sees who reported it. A "helpful" mark is kept as one row per comment and account and shown to nobody.
blogComments.audit: Every request that writes, edits, replies to or reports a comment records the connection's IP address in the request log (the "Request log" item above). It is never shown anywhere; it is kept only for a legal request or an abuse investigation.
blogComments.storage: Comments, reports and helpful marks are kept in our own database and sent to no third party.
blogComments.deletion: Deleting your account deletes all your comments — and the replies they received; your data export includes your comments.
blogComments.legalBasis: Legal basis: your own explicit action — you choose to comment.

aggregates.title: Aggregate response data (the sector table and a company page's "Response" tab)
aggregates.intro: The applications you track feed aggregate figures detached from your identity: a sector's or a company's response rate, first-reply time, post-interview silence and ghosting rate. When they do:
aggregates.what: Only the company, the application date, the status and the dates of status changes are aggregated. Your notes, HR contact, CV, e-mails and name never enter any aggregate.
aggregates.sector: The sector table is public and names no company. A sector row is not shown until at least 5 different people have 30 applications between them, and it stays closed while one person accounts for more than half of them.
aggregates.company: A company page's "Response" tab shows nothing until that company has at least 50 applications in the last 12 months, and nothing if one person accounts for more than a third of them; below the threshold it does not say how many are missing either. This tab stays off until the legal review is complete.
aggregates.noReverse: An aggregate cannot be walked back to one person's application: the pages show only rates, medians and a count of people, and individual application rows never leave the server.
aggregates.deletion: Deleting your account deletes your applications, and the next calculation drops them from the aggregates too (the tables are cached for at most an hour).
aggregates.legalBasis: Legal basis: legitimate interest — letting candidates see how much a sector or a company replies to applications; below the threshold no personal data is processed at all, above it it is shown only in aggregate.

terms.title: Terms of Use
terms.intro: This page sets out the rules that apply when you use e-kariyerim — the website, the Chrome extension and the tools that work without an account. By using the site you accept these terms; if you do not accept them, please do not use it. How your personal data is handled is described in a separate document, the Privacy Policy; the two apply together.

service.title: What the service is
service.intro: e-kariyerim is a tool for keeping track of your job search:
service.tracking: A dashboard that records your applications, tracked jobs and reminders; import from a LinkedIn export; a Chrome extension that collects signals from job pages and from replies in Gmail.
service.tools: Tools that work without an account: CV scan, reply-rate benchmark, and reading company reviews.
service.reviews: Public company pages where registered users write anonymous, structured reviews of companies.
service.salaries: Salary information: signed-in users share their salary at a company anonymously and read each other's entries.
service.asIs: The service is provided as is. We may change, pause or remove features; on a free service we do not promise advance notice, but a change that affects user data is announced on this page and, where needed, by email.
service.experiences: Candidate experiences, where signed-in users rate a company's hiring process from the candidate's side anonymously and anyone can read them.

account.title: Your account
account.age: You must be at least 18 to open an account.
account.accuracy: You open an account for yourself and are responsible for the information you give being accurate. Do not share an account with anyone or use someone else's.
account.security: Your password and your extension keys are your responsibility; anything done from your account counts as done by you. If you notice unauthorised use, change your password and write to us.
account.delete: You can delete your account permanently at any time from Account Settings; what gets deleted is listed in the Privacy Policy.

reviews.title: Company reviews
reviews.intro: Writing a company review needs an account and is subject to these rules:
reviews.ownExperience: You rate only what you experienced yourself — a company you worked at, interned at or went through the hiring process of. Do not rate hearsay, someone else's experience, or a company you have no relationship with.
reviews.structured: A review is made of ratings and fixed statements we wrote; there is no free text. The list of statements is the same for everyone and may be updated from time to time, like this page.
reviews.onePerCompany: You can write one review per company per account, and there is a cap on the total number per account; both are shown on the My Reviews page. If your view changes, you edit your existing review.
reviews.publication: Your review is published the moment you save it, without your name. If a reader reports it, a moderator looks at it and may leave it up, ask you for changes, or remove it; the reason appears on the My Reviews page. You can edit and resubmit a removed review; whether it goes back online is the moderator's decision.
reviews.noManipulation: Using reviews in an organised way to favour or harm a company — several accounts, reviews written for something in return, coordinated rating — is prohibited and leads to the account being closed.
reviews.opinion: Every published review is its author's personal opinion; it is not a statement by e-kariyerim about a company and we do not guarantee its accuracy.
reviews.companies: If you represent a company and believe a review about it breaks the rules, you can report that review or write to the address below.

salaries.title: Salary information
salaries.intro: When you share your salary at a company:
salaries.ownData: You share only your own salary; not someone else's, and not hearsay.
salaries.accurate: The amounts and the occupation you pick must be truthful.
salaries.signedInOnly: Entries are shown anonymously to signed-in users; readers see the occupation and an experience band, not your name.
salaries.quota: Ten entries per account in total, one per occupation at the same company. Deleting frees a slot.
salaries.opinion: Entries are user reports; e-kariyerim does not verify them, and they are not advice for salary negotiation.

experiences.title: Candidate experiences
experiences.intro: When you rate a company's hiring process:
experiences.ownProcess: You rate only a process you went through yourself; not on someone's behalf, not from hearsay.
experiences.structured: There is no free text: you rate and pick from ready-made statements. No interviewer, team or job title is asked; your entry does not point at a person.

scope.title: What this policy covers
scope.body: This page describes the e-kariyerim Browser Extension ("the extension") only. The extension is a companion to the e-kariyerim web application (ekariyerim.com): it lets a signed-in user save a job posting they are viewing — on LinkedIn, on kariyer.net, or on any other job site they choose to allow it on — as a tracked application in their own account, and offers an opt-in "Gmail Scanning" feature that checks an email you open in Gmail on your own device and only sends a short summary when it looks job-related. Data already saved to your account (your past applications) is governed by e-kariyerim's own privacy policy, not this document.

access.title: What the extension accesses, and when
access.intro: The extension does nothing until you click its toolbar icon. When you do, and only if the active tab is a job posting it is allowed to read, it reads:
access.item1: The job title, company name, and location visible on that page.
access.item2: The job description text and a formatted (bold/headings/lists) snapshot of it, visible on that page.
access.item3: The page's URL, to identify the job and detect duplicates.
access.item4: On a LinkedIn posting that publicly shows a hiring-team card: the name and public profile URL of the person who posted the job, offered as the contact for that application — so you know who to follow up with. Most postings don't show one (it is the poster's own choice), and nothing is filled in when they don't.
access.outro: Every field is shown to you, editable, in the extension's popup before anything is sent anywhere — including the contact, which you can change or clear before saving.

otherSites.title: Sites beyond LinkedIn and kariyer.net
otherSites.allow: LinkedIn and kariyer.net are the two sites the extension can read as installed. Anywhere else — Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workday, Workable, SmartRecruiters, a company's own careers page, a job board in your country — the popup shows an Allow button first, and Chrome asks you to confirm that one site before the extension can read anything there. Nothing is read on a site you have not allowed, and allowing one site says nothing about any other.
otherSites.markup: On those sites the extension reads the page's own schema.org job-posting markup: the structured description of the job that the page already publishes for search engines. If the page has none, nothing is filled in and you can still type the two fields yourself.
otherSites.remove: Every site you have allowed is listed in the extension's Settings page with a Remove button. Removing it stops the extension reading that site, immediately.

serverFetch.title: When a job posting is read a second time, on our servers
serverFetch.body: For a posting hosted on an applicant tracking system, e-kariyerim's own servers may afterwards request that posting from that system's public, unauthenticated job-board API, to fill in a description the page read could not reach — the text the CV-matching features need to work. The request contains the posting's own public address and nothing about you: no account, no cookie, no identifier. It happens on our servers after the application is saved, never in your browser, and only for these systems:
serverFetch.item5: Workday (the employer's own myworkdayjobs.com / myworkdaysite.com address)

gmail.title: Gmail Scanning (opt-in)
gmail.intro: Gmail Scanning turns status-update emails (interview invites, rejections, status updates) into suggestions without ever relaying your inbox anywhere. It is off by default. You turn it on yourself, per device, from the extension's Settings page.
gmail.whileOff: While off, nothing changes: the extension reads nothing on mail.google.com.
gmail.whenOn: Once turned on, whenever you personally open an email in Gmail, the extension reads that one message — sender address, subject line, and body text (capped at 2000 characters) — directly from the page, in your own browser. It never reads your inbox list, and never reads a message you haven't opened.
gmail.localScoring: That text is scored entirely on your device, against a small table of job-application-related keywords and known job-site/ATS domains, downloaded from e-kariyerim and cached locally. This table contains no personal data, only generic vocabulary and domain names.
gmail.whatIsSent: Only if that on-device score suggests the email is genuinely job-application-related does the extension send anything: the sender address, subject line, and the same capped snippet — never the full email body, and never anything about a message that didn't score as relevant — to your own e-kariyerim account, to be turned into a suggestion you can review. An email that scores as unrelated (which is most email — personal messages, receipts, newsletters, and so on) is never sent anywhere and is discarded the moment scoring finishes.
gmail.dedupe: The extension also keeps a small local list (on your device) of email threads it has already submitted, so re-opening the same email doesn't send a duplicate. This list, and the keyword table above, never leave your device except as the read-only fetch that downloads the table.

stored.title: What the extension stores
stored.intro: The extension stores the following locally on your device, using the browser's own chrome.storage.local (never Chrome Sync, never a third-party server):
stored.item1: The e-kariyerim API address you're using (a setting, not personal data).
stored.item2: The access token your e-kariyerim account issued to this extension, and the date it expires (so the extension can warn you before the connection lapses instead of simply stopping). It authenticates the extension's requests as you and reaches only the endpoints the extension uses — it cannot export your application history or manage your account. You obtain it by pressing "Connect" and confirming a code on your own account page; if you use a custom API address you can still generate one in e-kariyerim's Settings and enter it by hand.
stored.item3: Your light/dark theme preference for the extension's own popup.
stored.item4: Your language choice (Turkish/English) for the extension's pages.
stored.item5: Whether you've turned on Gmail Scanning (off unless you explicitly enable it), a cached copy of the (non-personal) keyword/domain table it scores against, and a short list of email thread IDs already submitted, so the same email isn't sent twice.
stored.outro: This data never leaves your device except as described in "What the extension sends, and to whom" below.

sent.title: What the extension sends, and to whom
sent.body: When you click "I Applied," the extension sends the job title, company, location, job URL, description and contact details shown in the popup to the e-kariyerim API, authenticated with your personal access token, so it can be saved to your own e-kariyerim account. Company-name autocomplete similarly queries the e-kariyerim API with the text you've typed.
sent.hrNote: A contact saved this way is your own note of who to approach about that application: only you can see it, it is never shown to other users or included in any analytics, e-kariyerim never emails or messages that person on your behalf, and it is deleted along with the application or your account.
sent.gmailNote: If you've turned on Gmail Scanning, an opened email that scores as job-related sends its sender, subject, and a capped snippet to your own e-kariyerim account (see the Gmail Scanning section above) — this only happens for emails you open, only after you enable the setting, and only when the on-device score qualifies.
sent.noOther: The extension sends data to no other destination. It does not use analytics, advertising, or tracking services, and it does not sell or share your data with third parties.
sent.pairing: When you press "Connect," the extension asks the e-kariyerim API for a pairing code and opens the confirmation page in a tab; while it waits it asks, every few seconds, whether you have confirmed that code. Neither request carries any personal data — the extension has no account and no credential at that point. The only thing that comes back is the access token, once, after you confirm. If you refuse on that page, or the code runs out of time, nothing is issued at all.

controls.title: Your controls
controls.item1: The job-tracking popup only acts when you click its icon — there is no background scraping or polling on any site, including the ones you allow.
controls.item2: Gmail Scanning is off by default and does nothing until you turn it on in Settings; once on, it only reads an email when you personally open it in Gmail — it does not scan your inbox in the background, and does nothing at all on any other site. Turn it off anytime in Settings, with the same immediate effect.
controls.item3: You can remove your access token at any time from the extension's Settings page, or revoke it from e-kariyerim's Settings → Browser Extension page, which invalidates it immediately. It also expires on its own after 90 days, whether or not you do anything.
controls.item4: Uninstalling the extension deletes everything chrome.storage.local held for it (the token, API address, theme, language preference, Gmail Scanning setting, and its local caches) from your device.
controls.item5: A pairing code is only ever an offer: it grants nothing until you confirm it while signed in, and the confirmation page has a "this wasn't me" button for a code you did not produce yourself.
controls.item6: A site you allowed can be taken back at any time from the extension's Settings page, which lists every one of them, or from Chrome's own extension settings.

intro.title: In short
intro.body: e-kariyerim uses only the two cookies the service needs to work. No advertising cookies, tracking pixels, analytics tools like Google Analytics, or any third-party cookies. That is why no cookie banner appears: there is no optional cookie to ask your consent for. The one exception is the Pro plan checkout: the payment form opens on PayTR's own page and PayTR may use its own strictly necessary cookies there; those cookies are not read on any other page of this site.
intro.legalNote: Under Turkish data protection law (KVKK), strictly necessary and functional cookies do not require explicit consent — what they require is disclosure. This page is that disclosure.

table.title: The cookies we use
table.name: Name
table.localePurpose: Remembers which language a page opens in (Turkish/English). Our server writes it to match the language in the address bar, and updates it when you switch languages.
table.localeDuration: Session: deleted when you close the browser
table.themePurpose: Remembers your light/dark theme preference. Written only when you press the theme button, or when you sign in and the preference stored on your account is applied.
table.note: Both store nothing but a preference: neither contains an identifier, a user number or a tracking code, and neither is sent to any third party.

storage.title: Browser storage (localStorage and sessionStorage)
storage.intro: These are not cookies, but they store data on your device in the same way, so we list them here too:
storage.item1: Session tokens — aa_access_token, aa_refresh_token, their expiry times, and aa_user (your name, email address and interface preferences). They keep you signed in; they live in localStorage and are deleted when you sign out.
storage.item2: Sign-in security keys — aa_google_oauth, aa_linkedin_oauth and aa_github_oauth. These are single-use values that block a CSRF attack during a Google, LinkedIn or GitHub sign-in; they live in sessionStorage and are deleted the moment the sign-in completes.
storage.outro: Both are required for the service to work — without them you cannot sign in.

visitCounter.title: Visit counter
visitCounter.intro: We count how often the site's public pages are opened, on our own server. No cookie is used, nothing is written to your browser, and nothing is sent to any third party. A visit adds only these three things to a counter:
visitCounter.item1: The address of the page opened — public pages only. Everything after the question mark (a search term, the key in a password-reset link) is cut off before it leaves your browser.
visitCounter.item2: The page's language — Turkish or English.
visitCounter.item3: Which site you found us from — the domain only (“google.com”, say), never the address on that site or the words you searched for.
visitCounter.note: None of this identifies you: no visitor id, no session id, no IP address and no browser details are stored. Two visits by the same person and one visit each by two people are therefore the same number to us, and a row can be linked neither to an account nor to another row. Even when you are signed in, this request carries none of your account's credentials.
visitCounter.noCookie: Because no cookie is written, the consent screen promised in “If this policy changes” below is not triggered here — that promise covers optional cookies. We are describing the counter anyway, so you can read what it holds.
visitCounter.dnt: If your browser has “Do Not Track” switched on, nothing is counted at all.
visitCounter.why: Why we count: there is no other way for us to see whether anyone arrives, which article is useful, or whether people who try to sign up get stuck. Counter rows are aggregate and hold no personal data, so they are kept indefinitely.

noThirdParty.title: Third parties and tracking
noThirdParty.intro: None of the following exist on this site:
noThirdParty.item1: Google Analytics, Meta Pixel, Hotjar or any comparable analytics/tracking tool.
noThirdParty.item3: Embedded third-party content (YouTube, Google Maps and the like) — we use none, so no cookies arrive behind them either.
noThirdParty.item4: Externally loaded fonts or scripts: fonts are bundled into our own server at build time, so your browser never calls Google Fonts.
noThirdParty.outro: The site's Content-Security-Policy only lets your browser connect to our own server, our own API and the error monitoring service; that list cannot grow quietly.

errorMonitoring.title: Error monitoring
errorMonitoring.before: We use Sentry so that we can diagnose unexpected errors. Sentry writes no cookie and stores nothing in your browser, but it does create a record when an error occurs. What is sent, where it goes and which legal basis it rests on is set out in detail in
errorMonitoring.link: the error monitoring section of the Privacy Policy
errorMonitoring.after: . Session replay and performance tracing are switched off; your browsing behaviour is not tracked.

control.title: How to remove cookies
control.body: You can delete this site's cookies and site data from your browser's settings at any time, and you can block cookies entirely. The effect: your language and theme preferences fall back to the defaults, and if you also delete the session tokens you are signed out and have to sign in again. Nothing else about the site stops working.
control.accountNote: Deleting the data held in your account is a separate matter — you can do that by deleting your account from the Settings page.

dashboard.intro: The Dashboard you land on after logging in summarizes your whole application process on one screen. The one-line summary under the heading gives you the three numbers that matter most, and the "New Application" button in the top right lets you add a new application directly.

hero.title: Open applications and the weekly trend
hero.body: The largest figure on the page is the total still waiting for a reply. The small chart beneath it shows how many applications you sent per week over the last 12 weeks. The four tiles beside it give your interview, offer, rejection and ghosting counts, each with its share of the total.

funnel.body: Shows how much of each stage made it to the next one along applied → replied → interview → offer. When the raw numbers are far apart (thousands of applications, a handful of interviews), every rail is still drawn at its own full width, so the small stages stay readable. The line underneath names the stage with the steepest drop-off.

responseTime.body: The median and average number of days from applying to first response, together with how many replied applications they were computed from. break.title: Taking a break
